title: Right to Equality
detail: The State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. This means the law applies equally to everyone, and everyone gets equal protection under it, regardless of status.
note: Foundational equality guarantee — applies to citizens and non-citizens alike within India.
_search: right to equality equal protection of laws

title: Prohibition of Discrimination
detail: The State shall not discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth. Special provisions can be made for women, children, and socially/educationally backward classes (including SC/ST/OBC), so reservation and welfare schemes for these groups are constitutionally protected, not exceptions to equality.
note: Article 15(3), (4), (5), (6) carve out permitted affirmative-action exceptions — do not present these as violations of equality.

title: Right to Freedom (Speech, Assembly, Movement, Profession)
detail: Guarantees six freedoms to citizens: freedom of speech and expression; to assemble peaceably without arms; to form associations or unions; to move freely throughout India; to reside and settle in any part of India; and to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade, or business. These are subject to 'reasonable restrictions' the State can impose (e.g. for public order, security, decency).
note: This article applies to citizens only, not to all persons (unlike Article 14 and 21).

title: Protection in Respect of Conviction for Offences
detail: No person can be convicted of an offence except for violating a law in force at the time the act was committed (no retrospective criminal law); no person can be punished more than once for the same offence (protection against double jeopardy); and no person accused of any offence can be compelled to be a witness against themselves (protection against self-incrimination).
note: Directly relevant to arrest and criminal-procedure questions — pairs well with Article 22 and CrPC/BNSS content.

title: Right to Life and Personal Liberty
detail: No person shall be deprived of their life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law. Indian courts have interpreted this expansively over the decades to include the right to live with dignity, right to privacy, right to a clean environment, right to health, right to education, and more.
note: One of the most litigated and broadly interpreted articles — applies to citizens and non-citizens (all 'persons').

title: Right to Education
detail: The State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years, in a manner the State may determine by law.
note: Inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment, 2002; implemented through the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009.

title: Protection Against Arrest and Detention
detail: A person who is arrested must be informed, as soon as possible, of the grounds for the arrest; has the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of their choice; and must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours of arrest (excluding travel time), and cannot be detained beyond that period without the magistrate's authority.
note: This is the core constitutional basis for 'what are my rights if arrested' questions — pair with CrPC/BNSS arrest-procedure detail and the IPC/BNS note where relevant.

title: Prohibition of Traffic in Human Beings and Forced Labour
detail: Traffic in human beings, begar (forced labour without payment), and other similar forms of forced labour are prohibited, and any contravention is an offence punishable by law.
note: Basis for anti-trafficking and bonded-labour protections.

title: Prohibition of Child Labour
detail: No child below the age of 14 years shall be employed to work in any factory, mine, or other hazardous employment.
note: Reinforced by the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act.

title: Freedom of Religion
detail: All persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right to freely profess, practise, and propagate religion, subject to public order, morality, health, and other fundamental rights.
note: Applies to all persons, not just citizens.

title: Right to Constitutional Remedies
detail: Guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights, through writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, and certiorari. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called this 'the heart and soul of the Constitution.'
note: This is the enforcement mechanism for all other Fundamental Rights — relevant when explaining how a person can actually act on a rights violation.

title: Free Legal Aid
detail: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall provide free legal aid to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities.
note: A Directive Principle (not directly enforceable like Fundamental Rights), but it is the constitutional basis for NALSA and the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 — cite this when pointing users to free legal aid.
